261.quote_or_event: “Suffering from insects a great sage remains undisturbed. … Tolerate living beings, do not kill them, though they eat your flesh and blood.”
261.explanation: In the lecture on the twenty-two troubles (parīṣaha) a monk must bear, Mahavira tells him to endure even the bites of insects without driving them off or harming them.
261.tie_back: Valluvar defines penance as bearing one's own suffering while causing none to others; this verse joins exactly those two halves, patient endurance and refusal to injure even the creatures causing the pain.
261._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (ellipsis omits the elephant simile and one clause); a near one-to-one fit, since the Jain parīṣaha discipline pairs endurance with ahimsa just as the Kural does.

262.quote_or_event: “If an ignorant man should eat but a blade of Kusa-grass every month, (the merit of his penance) will not equal the sixteenth part of his who possesses the Law as it has been taught.”
262.explanation: King Nami tells Indra that even the most extreme fasting by one who lacks right understanding is worth almost nothing beside the inner possession of the true Law.
262.tie_back: The Kural says outward tapas is futile for those who lack its inner quality; Nami makes the same point by ranking the severest fast of an ignorant man below a sixteenth of true inner discipline.
262._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified in 'Kusa'); a strong fit on futile outward austerity, though it does not reproduce the Kural's karmic reading that tapas comes only to those with past merit.

263.quote_or_event: “You have left the dreadful âsrama (that of the householder) and are wanting to enter another; (remain what you were), O king, and be content with observing the Pôsaha-days.”
263.explanation: Indra, testing Nami, suggests he stay a householder and keep only the lay fasting days (pōṣadha), reflecting the Jain arrangement in which lay people support monks with alms while practising lesser austerities themselves.
263.tie_back: Valluvar ironically asks whether householders forgot penance because they were busy feeding renunciants; the Jain scheme answers differently, expecting even householders to keep periodic fasts alongside their almsgiving.
263._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics as printed there); next-best only, since no Jain text echoes Valluvar's irony, and Jainism actually expects laity to practise some tapas rather than excusing them.

264.quote_or_event: “He is the man of great fame and might, of awful piety and power; do not injure him who cannot be injured, lest he consume you all by the fire (of his virtue).”
264.explanation: When Brahmin youths beat the outcaste-born monk Harikesa, Bhadra warns them of his ascetic power and Yakshas strike them down, yet Harikesa himself declares, 'There is not the least hatred in me' (12.32).
264.tie_back: The Kural credits tapas with power to crush foes and raise up friends; the Harikesa story shows that power vividly, though in Jain telling the monk himself wills no harm.
264._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a good narrative match for the power of tapas, but Jain ethics denies that the ascetic should will an enemy's destruction, which the Kural allows.

265.quote_or_event: “As a large tank, when its supply of water has been stopped, gradually dries up by the consumption of the water and by evaporation, so the Karman of a monk, which he acquired in millions of births, is annihilated by austerities, if there is no influx of bad Karman.”
265.explanation: Jain doctrine holds that tapas, once new karmic inflow is stopped, burns away accumulated karma (nirjarā), and so is the decisive means to liberation.
265.tie_back: Valluvar urges penance now because it obtains what one desires; the Jain text also presents tapas as supremely effective, but its goal is the shedding of karma rather than the fulfilment of wishes.
265._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; partial fit, since Jainism explicitly rejects performing penance for desired worldly results (nidāna), so only the 'tapas is effective' idea carries over.

266.quote_or_event: “Pleasures are the thorn that rankles, pleasures are poison, pleasures are like a venomous snake; he who is desirous of pleasures will not get them, and will come to a bad end at last.”
266.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his throne, warns Indra that the pursuit of pleasure is self-destructive and ends in ruin.
266.tie_back: Valluvar contrasts ascetics doing their true work with those who, caught in the net of desire, labour for their own ruin; Nami's verse gives the second half of that contrast in the strongest terms.
266._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a strong fit for the desire-brings-ruin half of the couplet, while the 'own proper work' half is only implied by Nami's renunciation.

267.quote_or_event: “He who is exempt from love, hatred, and fear, (and who shines forth) like burnished gold, purified in fire, him we call a Brâhmana.”
267.explanation: The monk Jayaghosha describes the true holy man as one whose passions have been burnt away, so that he shines like gold refined in fire.
267.tie_back: Valluvar's image of gold that shines brighter the more it is heated is matched here by the same goldsmith's image for the ascetic purified of passion.
267._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com (diacritics simplified); the gold-in-fire image is close, though Jacobi's footnote notes the compound may instead mean 'whose impurities and sins had been annihilated', and the verse lacks the Kural's emphasis on suffering.

268.quote_or_event: “Happy are we, happy live we who call nothing our own; when Mithilâ is on fire, nothing is burned that belongs to me.”
268.explanation: Nami, having given up his kingdom, is free of every sense of 'mine'; at the end of the dialogue Indra himself reveals his true form and pays reverence to him again and again (9.59).
268.tie_back: The Kural says one free of 'I' and 'mine' is worshipped by all beings; Nami shows that freedom from possession, and the king of the gods bows before him.
268._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; strong on freedom from 'mine' and, through Indra's reverence, on being worshipped, though the verse speaks of possessions more than of the ego 'I'.

269.quote_or_event: “If a sage truly performs these two kinds of austerities, he will soon be thoroughly released from the Circle of Births.”
269.explanation: After listing the six external and six internal austerities, the lecture promises that their true practice frees the soul entirely from repeated birth and death.
269.tie_back: Valluvar says the power of tapas lets one leap even beyond Death; for Jainism, austerity ends the cycle of birth and death altogether, so death no longer has a hold.
269._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; good thematic fit, though the Jain text speaks of release from rebirth rather than escaping a personified Death (Yama).

270.quote_or_event: “And though they have heard the Law and believe in it, it is difficult for them to fulfill it strenuously; many who approve of the religion, do not adopt it.”
270.explanation: The 'four requisites' lecture says that human birth, hearing the Law, faith and strenuous practice are each rare, so very few actually carry the discipline through.
270.tie_back: Valluvar says the many are destitute because those who practise penance are few; the Jain text likewise laments that many approve the path but few take it up.
270._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; matches the 'few practise, many do not' arithmetic, but does not link that scarcity to worldly poverty as the Kural does.
